transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-held key because OLT's delivered TMS API leaves no other option. It authenticates with a single global `x-api-key` header, and it has no user login, no login endpoint and no per-user credential. ADR-001 therefore rejects Option A, where each user forwards their own TMS credential. That option is structurally impossible, because customers have no TMS credential to present. It also rejects Option B, where re:cinq exchanges or holds per-user credentials, because none exist to exchange or hold. Option C is the only option the published API supports. Under it, Otto holds one global `TMS_API_KEY`, and Otto's own code enforces OLT's requirement that customers see only their own bookings. The TMS cannot tell customers apart, so Otto derives the customer number server-side from the verified token. `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` does this on every call. The model never supplies a customer identifier as a tool input. Each TMS tool also runs an ownership check. The ADR's holds_when table says this conclusion holds only while the API stays key-only. Whether the TMS can scope a key to a single customer is still an open question (OC-1).

judgements.reason: The answer covers the single global TMS_API_KEY, the customer boundary enforced in Otto's code, and the TMS having no user-level auth. It omits the gold's point that per-user credentials are moot because the TMS issues one key per integration partner.
